title: Rohit Sharma's Match-Night Comfort Food: His Mother's Banana Wafers
excerpt: The former India captain revealed on his new show 'Family Full House' that Test-match nerves kept him awake at night — and that his mother's homemade, baked banana wafers were the comfort food he always carried with him.
body:
• Rohit Sharma revealed on his new show 'Family Full House with Rohit Sharma' that nervousness before Test matches often kept him awake through the night.
  • His go-to comfort food during those sleepless nights: homemade banana wafers, baked — not fried — by his mother, which he always carried with him on tour.
  • The former India captain retired from Tests last year after 67 matches, scoring 4,301 runs with 12 centuries and 18 fifties at an average of 40.57.
  • The show premiered on September 19 on Sony Entertainment Television and Sony LIV, with Sharma speaking candidly about his career and personal life.

Former India captain Rohit Sharma has revealed the unlikely comfort food that saw him through sleepless nights during Test matches: his mother's homemade banana wafers. For all his calm at the crease, the opener says the pressure of his favourite format often left him nervous and craving a late-night snack.

"Main jhooth nahi bolunga"

Speaking on the premiere episode of his television show, 'Family Full House with Rohit Sharma', the 38-year-old admitted that Test cricket unsettled him more than any other format. "Yes, those cravings used to happen. I would not lie. When I would play Tests, I would feel nervous. It was my favourite format," he said in Hindi, opening with the phrase 'Main jhooth nahi bolunga' — I will not lie. He explained that the demands of the longest format made it difficult to switch off after a day's play: the nervousness simply would not let him sleep, and he would stay awake through the night.

Baked, not fried

Staying awake brought its own urges. "When you are awake, you feel like eating something or the other," he said. "So I always kept my comfort food with me, which my mother always made for me — banana wafers." The snack came with a personal touch: his mother baked the wafers rather than frying them, a method all her own, and he carried a supply with him wherever Tests took him. "Whenever I felt like it, I would just eat them."

"Yes, those cravings used to happen. I would not lie. When I would play Tests, I would feel nervous. It was my favourite format."

— Rohit Sharma, on 'Family Full House'

A career in the longest format

Rohit played 67 Tests for India between 2013 and 2024, scoring 4,301 runs at an average of 40.57, with 12 centuries and 18 fifties and a highest score of 212. He called time on his Test career last year, ending a red-ball journey that began in fits and starts before blossoming into one of India's most dependable overseas records.

The taste of home

Banana wafers — thin, crisp slices of raw banana — are a fixture of Indian tea-time tables, most famously the fried Kerala-style chips. The baked version is his mother's own recipe, a quieter, lighter take on a familiar snack. It is easy to see why the story resonates: for a player spending months on the road, a mother's cooking is the one taste that cannot be replicated in a hotel kitchen.

Following the story

For the diaspora, Rohit's confession lands in familiar territory — the immigrant's lifelong negotiation between a mother's kitchen and everything that came after. Comfort food, for millions of Indian families abroad, is less about the recipe than about who made it. New episodes of 'Family Full House with Rohit Sharma' air on Sony Entertainment Television and stream on Sony LIV.
